Abstract
Background & Aims: Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a major cause of chronic liver 
disease. The precise role of NK cells in the progression of NASH has yet to be elucidated. 
Methods: By using methionine-choline deficient diets (MCD)-induced NASH model, the role of 
NK cells was identified in WT mice compared with conventional NK cell-deficient Nfil3-/- mice. 
Results: After 8 weeks of MCD-treatment, NASH was induced as shown by the significant 
macrovesicular steatosis, necro-inflammation and fibrosis in the liver of WT B6 mice. In 
MCD-treated WT B6 mice, the number of NK cells was markedly increased in the liver, but 
decreased in the spleen. Intrahepatic NK cells exhibited high levels of activation, as evidenced by 
the expression of CD107a and cytokine production of IFN-γ, TGF- and IL-10. Lower expression 
levels of Ki67 indicated a reduction in the proliferation of intrahepatic NK cells after 
MCD-treatment. Increased expression of CXCL10 in the liver early after MCD-treatment led to 
the increased recruitment of CXCR3+ NK cells into the liver. The MCD-treated Nfil3-/- mice 
showed similar levels of TG and macrovesicular steatosis, however more inflammatory infiltration 
and increased collagen deposition in the liver. Further, the depletion of NK cells during

MCD-induced NASH caused a significant increase in the infiltration of monocyte-derived 
macrophages (MoMFs) particularly Ly6Clo subsets towards M2. Conclusions: Intrahepatic NK 
cells, recruited through CXCL10-CXCR3 interaction, play a protective role against the fibrosis 
progression in NASH, which provide us with a better understanding of the immunopathogenesis of 
NASH. 
Key words: non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, liver fibrosis, natural killer cell, CXCL10, CXCR3
Lay Summary: By using an MCD-induced NASH model, NK cells were found to be recruited 
into the liver via interaction between CXCL10 and CXCR3. The intrahepatic NK cells were 
activated and played a protective role against the progression of fibrosis in NASH. 
Introduction
Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a major cause of chronic liver disease, and is 
characterized by intense intrahepatic inflammation, exacerbated steatosis, hepatocellular injury 
and incipient fibrosis, which can develop progressive liver fibrosis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular 
carcinoma (HCC) 1. Approximately 20% of patients with NASH are known to eventually progress 
to cirrhosis; and of these approximately 8% develop a potentially fatal liver disease, such as liver 
cancer 2. The precise pathogenesis of NASH remains obscure and has yet to be elucidated, 
although previous research suggested that activation of the immune system may contribute to the 
progression of NASH 3. 
Oxidative stress can contribute to the progression of NASH by stimulating both humoral and 
cellular immune responses, thus indicating the possible role of adaptive immunity in the 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved
pathogenesis of this disease 4. The selective loss of CD4+ T cells was induced during NASH since 
increased free fatty acid destroyed the electron transport chain and induced the release of reactive 
oxygen species (ROS), thus promoting the development of NASH-HCC 5. By choline-deficient 
high-fat diet (CD-HFD) treatment, metabolic activation of intrahepatic CD8+ T cells and NKT 
cells, but not myeloid cells were demonstrated to promote NASH and liver cancer by interactions 
with hepatocytes 6. During NASH, NKT cells were accumulated via a process regulated by 
Hedgehog (Hh), and then promoted the activation of hepatic stellate cell (HSC) to become 
myofibroblasts (MFs). Cirrhotic livers harbored large numbers of NKT cells. Hepatic NKT cells 
derived production of OPN and hedgehog (Hh) ligands that promoted fibrogenesis during NASH 
7,8. Tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) produced by activated Kupffer cells (KCs) is essential for 
triggering the development of NASH and liver fibrosis 9,10. In the absence of KCs, NASH is 
mitigated in mice fed a methionine-choline deficient diet (MCD) 11. On the other hand, dendritic 
cells (DCs) played a regulatory role in NASH by limiting sterile inflammation, as demonstrated 
via their role in the clearance of apoptotic cells and necrotic debris 12. DC also limited CD8+ T cell 
expansion and restricted Toll-like receptor expression and cytokine production in innate immune 
effector cells in NASH, including KCs, neutrophils, and inflammatory monocytes 12.
Liver is a lymphoid organ with an overwhelming number of innate immune cells 13,14. The 
population of NK cells in the liver is particularly enriched and accounts for 30-50% and 5-10% 
of hepatic lymphocytes in human and mouse, respectively 15. As a key component of innate 
immunity in the liver, NK cells not only play an important role in controlling viral hepatitis, 
liver fibrosis and liver tumorigenesis, but also contribute to the pathogenesis of liver injury and 
inflammation 14,16. However, the role of NK cells in NASH has yet to be fully elucidated. In a 
previous study of spontaneous NASH in glycine N-methyltransferase (GNMT)-/- mice, 
TRAIL-producing NK cells actively contributed to promote a proinflammatory environment 
during early stages of fatty liver disease, thus suggesting that this cell compartment may 
contribute to the progression of NASH 17. Conversely, NKp46+ NK cells played an important 
role in preventing NASH progression to fibrosis by regulating the M1/M2 polarization of liver 
macrophages (Mϕ) 18. 
In C57BL/6 mice, NASH-like liver pathology can be induced by MCD diets, mimicking the 
severe form of NASH with fibrosis that occurs in some humans 19. In this study, we used a mouse 
model of NASH induced MCD and demonstrated that during NASH NK cells were recruited into 
the liver in a CXCL10-CXCR3 manner, and attenuated the inflammatory infiltration and fibrosis

progression. These findings provide us with a better understanding of the role of NK cells in the 
progression of NASH.   
Materials and methods
Animals. Six-8 week-old male C57BL/6 mice were obtained from the Shanghai Experimental 
Center of the Chinese Science Academy (Shanghai, China). Nfil3-/- mice were a gift from Dr. Tak 
Mak (University of Toronto, Canada). All mice were maintained under specific-pathogen-free 
(SPF) controlled conditions (22°C, 55% humidity, and 12 h day/night rhythm) in compliance with 
the guidelines outlined in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. The study was 
ethically approved by the Animal Use and Management Committee of the University of Science 
and Technology of China (Approval number USTCACUC1801071).
MCD-induced NASH model. Methionine- and choline deficient diet (MCD) (Trophic Animal 
Feed High-Tech Co.,Ltd, China) were used to induce NASH model. Methionine- and choline 
sufficient diet (MCS) (Trophic Animal Feed High-Tech Co.,Ltd, China) was used as the control 
diet. Mice were fed with MCD or MCS diet for a total period of 8 weeks. During this period, the 
diets were changed every 2 days. Body weight was monitored weekly. Triglyceride (TG) levels 
were detected using a Triglycerides Assay Kit (Huili, China). 
Serum transaminase activity assays. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate 
aminotransferase (AST) activities were detected using the serum transaminase test kit (Rong 
Sheng, Shanghai, China) and an automated Chemray 240 clinical analyzer (Rayto, Shenzen, 
China). 
Histological examination. Liver samples were fixed in 12% neutral-buffered formalin and 
embedded in paraffin. Sections (5 μm) were then prepared and stained with hematoxylin and eosin 
using routine methods. Collagen analysis was performed by Sirius Red staining. The proportion of 
adipose vacuoles area in liver was calculated using Image-Pro (Media Cybernetics, Inc.). The 
number of inflammation foci was calculated per field (at a magnification of 100×) in 10 fields. For 
immunohistochemistry analysis, reagents included anti-CD11b (GB11058, 
Wuhan Servicebio Technology, China), anti-F4/80 (GB11027, Wuhan Servicebio Technology, 
China) and biotinylated anti-mouse IgG (PV6000, ZSGB-bio, Beijing, China). The sections were

photographed using an Pannoramic DESK (3D HISTECH) with the software Pannoramic Scanner.
Preparation of mononuclear cells (MNCs). Liver and spleen MNCs were isolated as described 
previously 20. In brief, the liver MNCs were isolated with 40% and 70% Percoll solutions 
(GIBCOL BRL, Grand Island, NY) with centrifugation at 1260 g for 30 min at room temperature. 
Splenocytes were treated with RBC lysis solution (BD PharMingen, San Diego, CA).
Flow cytometry analysis. After blocking with 10 μl of rat serum for 30 min at 4°C, MNCs were 
stained with the indicated fluorescence-labeled monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) for the surface 
antigens at 4 ℃ for 30 min in darkness. For the intracellular assay, freshly isolated cells were 
stimulated with 50 ng/mL of PMA (Sigma, St Louis, MO) and 1 μg/mL of ionomycin (Sigma, St 
Louis, MO), and treated with 10 μg/mL of monensin (Sigma, St Louis, MO) for 4h. After staining 
the surface antigens, the cells were fixed and permeabilized using 100 μL of Cytofix and 
Cytoperm solution (eBioscience, San Diego, CA). An LSR II-flow cytometer or LSR Fortessa 
(BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA) was used and the data were analyzed using FlowJo (Tree Star). 
The mAbs include FITC-CD69, FITC-CD107a, Alex647-Ki67, PE-IL-10, BUV737-CD11b (BD 
PharMingen, San Diego, CA); PE-NKG2A, APC- NKG2D, APC-F4/80 (eBioscience, San Diego, 
CA), BV786-IFN-γ, PerCP-Cy5.5-CD3,PE-Cy7-NK1.1, BV421-CXCR3, BV421-TGF-β, 
APC-Cy7-CD45, and BV605-Ly6C (BioLegend, San Diego, CA). 
Real-time quantitative PCR. Total RNA was extracted from liver tissue using TRIZOL reagent 
(Invitrogen). Gene expression was analyzed according to the instructions of the SYBR Premix Ex 
Taq kit (Takara) and quantified using the ΔΔCt method. All primers were synthesized by Sangon 
(Shanghai, China). The primers are as followed: cxcl9 forward (P1)

Cell depletion. Anti-asGM1 (50μL/mouse; Wako Pure Chemical Industries, Ltd. Japan) was 
injected intraperitoneally (ip.) twice a week to deplete NK cells in the body. One day prior to 
MCD-treatment, the mice were injected with anti-asGM1.
Detection of CXCL10 protein. The levels of CXCL10 protein in the serum and liver tissues were 
determined by a mouse CXCL10 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit (BMS6018, 
Invitrogen) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Liver samples were homogenized 
in ice-cold NP40 lysis buffer containing 1mM PMSF and protease inhibitor cocktail (Complete 
Mini; Roche, Basel, Switzerland). Samples were then centrifuged at 15000 g for 10 min at 4 °C 
and the supernatant was retained for analysis. 
In vitro migration assay. NK cells were purified from splenic MNCs by negative selection using 
an NK Cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany). A range of concentrations of 
the chemokine CXCL10 (IP-10) (Pepro Tech, USA) were added to the bottom of chambers of 
24-well Transwell plate (6.5 μm pore size; Corning Costar). NK cells (2.5×105) in a total volume 
of 100 μL 1640 medium were added to the Transwell inserts above the chamber and incubated at 
37℃ for 4 h in 5% CO2 and then for 30 min at 4℃ to loosen leukocytes that had bound to the 
undersides of the membranes. The cells in the lower chambers were then collected and counted in 
a Neubauer hemocytometer. The chemotaxis index was calculated by dividing the number of cells 
migrating in response to CXCL10 stimulation by the number of cells migrating in wells containing 
control medium.
Statistical analysis. All data are shown as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Data were

analyzed using the Student’s t test or analysis of variance (ANOVA) as appropriate. P < 0.05 was 
considered to be statistically significant.
Results
1. MCD diets induce NASH and liver fibrosis in wild type B6 mice
Compared with control MCS diets, MCD-treated mice gradually lost their body weight (Figure 
1A), and developed significant macrovesicular steatosis and ballooning degeneration of 
hepatocytes (Figure 1B). Higher levels of TG were identified in the livers of MCD-treated mice, 
thus indicating a higher severity of steatosis (Fig 1C). In addition, necro-inflammation was 
observed in the livers of MCD-treated mice (Figure 1B); this observation was further 
demonstrated by significant increases in the serum levels of ALT and AST of MCD-treated mice 
(Figure 2A). Increased levels of collagen deposition shown by Sirius Red staining indicated the 
liver fibrosis progression after 8 weeks of MCD-treatment (Figure 2B). 
2. NK cells are markedly accumulated and activated in the livers of MCD-induced NASH 
mice
Liver MNCs were isolated and analyzed by flow cytometry to determine the percentages and 
number of NK cells. NK cells accounted for 5~10% of the intrahepatic lymphocytes in the control 
mice (Figure 3A and B). Two weeks of MCD diet feeding resulted in a significant enrichment of 
NK cells in the livers with higher percentages and numbers compared to the control mice (Figure 
3A), and this trend continued over the entire 8 weeks of MCD diet feeding (Figure 3B). In 
comparison, there was a reduction in the number of NK cells in the spleen at 2 and 8 weeks of 
MCD-treatment, suggesting that NK cells had been recruited from the peripheral lymphoid organs 
into the liver as a result of the MCD-treatment (Figure 3A and B). Furthermore, these intrahepatic 
NK cells were activated with higher expression levels of CD69, but not the splenic NK cells 
(Figure 3C). The expression levels of inhibitory receptor NKG2A were significantly upregulated 
on intrahepatic NK cells, while activated receptor NKG2D and cytotoxic molecule TRAIL were 
downregulated. These accumulated intrahepatic NK cells produced higher levels of CD107a, 
IFN-γ, TGF- and IL-10 after MCD treatment, which was distinguished from that of the spleen 
with weak expression of TGF-  and IL-10 (Figure 3C). 
3. NK cells are recruited into the liver in CXCL10-CXCR3-dependent manner
Further, we determined the proliferation of intrahepatic NK cells during MCD-induced NASH.

Lower levels of Ki67 expression were observed in intrahepatic and splenic NK cells after 2 weeks 
of MCD treatment (Fig 4A), indicating that the increased number of NK cells in the liver was not 
a consequence of cell proliferation. Until to 8 weeks of MCD treatment, similar results of the 
expression levels of Ki67 in NK cells were observed (Fig 4B). We also determined the expressions 
of several kinds of chemokines associated to NK cell migration to investigate the accumulation of 
NK cells in the liver induced by the MCD diet. As shown in Figure 5A, 8 weeks after MCD 
treatment the mRNA expression levels of CXC-chemokine ligand (cxcl)9, cxcl10 and cxcl11 were 
significantly increased in the liver. Notably, only cxcl10 mRNA showed an increase in hepatic 
expression during weeks 1-4 of MCD treatment, but not cxcl9 and cxcl11 (Figrure 5A), indicating 
that chemokine CXC-chemokine ligand 10 (CXCL 10) may be responsible for the recruitment of 
NK cells into the liver during the early phases of MCD-induced NASH. The significant increase in 
the expression levels of CXCL10 protein in liver tissue after 2 weeks of MCD treatment further 
suggested the critical role of CXCL10 in the pathogenesis of NASH (Figure 5B). C-X-C motif 
receptor 3 (CXCR3) is the only known receptor for CXCL10. Consequently, more CXCR3+ NK 
cells were recruited into the liver during MCD-treatment (Fig 5C). Furthermore, CXCL10 
exhibited the capacity to mediate the chemotaxis of NK cells, shown by an in vitro migration 
assay (Figure 5D), thus indicating that the recruitment of NK cell into the liver was dependent on 
CXCL10 during MCD-induced NASH. 
4. Deficiency of NK cells causes a loss in protective function against hepatic fibrosis in Nfil3-/- 
mice
Nfil3-/- mice that are deficient in conventional NK cells in their body were used to investigate the 
role of NK cells during MCD-induced NASH. Compared with wild type (WT) B6 mice, Nfil3-/- 
mice showed a much more severe loss of body weight after 8 weeks of MCD-treatment (Figure 6 
A). There was no significant difference in the levels of hepatic TG between Nfil3-/- and WT B6 
mice 8 weeks after MCD-treatment (Figure 6B), which was further confirmed by the similar 
histological features of macrovesicular steatosis (Figure 6 C and D). However, a greater extent of 
inflammatory infiltration was observed in the livers of MCD-treated Nfil3-/- mice, as evidenced by 
an increased number of inflammatory foci per field compared with MCD-treated WT B6 mice 
(Figure 6 C and E). When NK cells were depleted in WT B6 mice by anti-asGM1 antibody, there 
was a greater accumulation of MNCs in the liver, but not the spleen (Fig 6F), further 
demonstrating that NK cells inhibited hepatic inflammation, but not hepatosteatosis during

MCD-induced NASH.
Furthermore, similar increases in the serum levels of ALT and AST were determined in 
MCD-treated Nfil3-/- mice and MCD-treated WT B6 mice (Figure 7A), indicating that there was 
no significant difference in the hepatocyte injury between Nfil3-/- and WT B6 mice after MCD 
treatment. However, aggravated liver fibrosis was observed in MCD-treated Nfil3-/- mice, shown 
by increased levels of collagen deposition in the liver by Sirius Red staining (Figure 7B). These 
results indicated that NK cells attenuated fibrosis progression of NASH. 
5. Monocyte-derived macrophages are induced and polarized toward M2 in the absence of 
NK cells
Next, the accumulated MNCs in the liver were further analyzed by flow cytometry to identify the 
cell population that exhibited cross-talk with NK cells. After 17 days of MCD-treatment, the 
percentages and numbers of CD45+ CD11bhi F4/80int monocyte-derived macrophages (MoMFs) 
were significantly increased in NK cell-depleted mice compared with control mice (Figure 8A). 
The increased infiltration of MoMFs in the livers of NK cell-depleted mice was further confirmed 
by the histochemical analysis of CD11b+ and F4/80+ cells (Figure 8B). Among these MoMFs, 
higher proportion of Ly6Clo and a rise in the number of Ly6Clo MoMFs were further observed in 
the absence of NK cells (Figure 8A). Since M2 macrophages express low levels of Ly6C 
compared with M1 macrophages, we therefore evaluated the relative expression levels of M1 and 
M2 markers in this population of MoMFs. MCD treatment upregulated the expression of M1 
markers, including ly6c, ifn-γ, tnf-α and nos2, which were significantly reduced upon the depletion 
of NK cells (Figure 8C). Alternatively, the expression of M2 markers, including il-10, il-4, tgf-β 
and retnla, were significantly enhanced upon the depletion of NK cells (Figure 8C). These results 
indicated that the hepatic population of MoMFs were induced and skewed towards M2 in the 
absence of NK cells during MCD-induced NASH.
Discussion 
In this study, we demonstrated that NK cells were markedly recruited into the liver in 
CXCL10-CXCR3 manner during MCD-induced NASH, and these intrahepatic NK cells 
attenuated the fibrosis progression of NASH. MCD-induced NASH in an animal model replicates 
the severe form of NASH with fibrosis that occurs in some humans with no obesity. Among 
NASH patients, approximately 30% are non-obese, while the other 70% are with obesity. Here we 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved
presented evidence to support the protective role of NK cells in a model of NASH with no obesity, 
which provide us with a better understanding of the immunopathogenesis of NASH. 
The number of hepatic NK cells was markedly increased in obese patients with NASH 
compared to normal healthy control, along with higher expression levels of NK cell-associated 
cytotoxic mediators (such as TRAIL, NKG2D, and MICA/B), suggesting that NK cells are 
activated and contribute to the pathogenesis of NASH 21. In this study, activation of intrahepatic 
NK cells was also observed, but with lower levels of TRAIL expression (Figure 3C), suggesting 
the possibility that NK cells may play different roles in this particular animal model. By using 
Nfil3-/- mice that are deficient in conventional NK cells, we demonstrated that conventional NK 
cells prevented the fibrosis progression (Figure 7B). This finding was consistent with a previous 
finding that NKp46+DX5+ NK cells limited NASH progression to fibrosis 18. NK cells can 
selectively kill activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) to curtail the development of fibrosis 22, and 
can also regulate fibrosis by modulating the fibrogenic properties of other immune cells resident in 
the liver 15. As reported previously, NKp46+ NK cells regulated M1 polarization of liver Mϕ via 
the production of IFN-γ to exhibit their protective role against liver fibrosis 18. Consistently, 
increased production of IFN-γ in intrahepatic NK cells was detected during MCD-induced NASH 
(Figure 3C), and expression levels of IFN-γ in the liver were significantly decreased upon the 
depletion of NK cells (Figure 8C). A recent study also reported the protective role of IFN-γ in the 
NASH with obesity 23. However, the production of TGF- and IL-10 was also upregulated in the 
intrahepatic NK cells (Figure 3C). TGF-β signaling in hepatocytes contributed to hepatocyte death 
and lipid accumulation via Smad signaling and ROS production that promoted the development 
of NASH and NASH progression to fibrosis 23,24. The roles of these cytokines should be further 
investigated to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the role of NK cells in NASH. 
Further studies are required to clarify the cross-talk between NK cells and other immune cells 
in the liver during NASH. Since a greater level of immune cell infiltration was detected in 
MCD-treated mice following the depletion of NK cells (Figure 6F), the specific subsets of cells 
involved were further investigated in this study. A significantly greater proportion of CD45+ 
CD11bhi F4/80int MoMFs were induced in the absence of NK cells in the liver during 
MCD-induced NASH, and this subset of cells were skewed towards M2 (Figure 8). These results 
indicated that NK cells attenuated the fibrosis progression of NASH by regulating liver Mϕ and 
their polarization. NK cells might directly or indirectly inhibit certain immune cells by producing 
specific cytokines as described above. There are two distinct NK cell subsets in the liver: 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved
liver-resident NK cells (CD49a+CD49b-) and conventional NK cells (CD49a-CD49b+) with 
distinct phenotypical and developmental features 25,26. We considered that the respective roles of 
liver-resident NK cells (LrNK) and conventional NK cells (cNK) deserved further investigation 
during the progression of NASH. Given that Nfil3-/- mice are deficient in cNK cells but not LrNK 
cells, our present data indicated that cNK cells played a protective role in the inflammation and 
fibrosis progression of NASH (Figure 6E and 7B).   
The chemokine CXCL10 exhibits potent chemotactic capacity for cells expressing its cognate 
receptor CXCR3 27. In this study, we found that MCD treatment significantly increased the 
expression of CXCL10 in the liver, consequently with the increased CXCR3+ NK cells in the liver 
(Figure 5), indicating the critical role of CXCL10 in the recruitment of NK cells. Clinical studies 
of NASH have reported significantly higher levels of circulating and hepatic CXCL10 in patients 
28. However, the blockade of CXCL10 resulted in protection against the development of 
steatohepatitis in mice, which was similar to the findings in CXCL10-/- mice with reduced liver 
steatosis, injury, inflammation, and fibrosis 28. Since several types of innate immune cells are 
known to express CXCR3 including KCs, DCs, NK, NKT and neutrophils, the specific role of 
CXCL10 is likely to be complex 29,30. By using CXCL10-/- mice, macrophage-associated 
inflammation appeared to be the key player in the CXCL10-mediated sterile inflammatory 
response in NASH, but not the other innate immune cells 30. Conditional knockout of CXCR3 
receptor in specific cell subsets will help to elucidate the exact role of these cells. In addition to 
CXCL10, CXCR3 is the cognate receptor of CXCL9 and CXCL11, and consequently there may 
be some redundancy in its binding to CXCL10 31. The expression of CXCL9 and CXCL11 did not 
change significantly in the livers of MCD-treated mice between weeks 1-4 of MCD-treatment 
(Figure 5A), which indicated that the recruitment of CXCR3+ NK cells was predominantly 
dependent on the increased expression of CXCL10 in the liver. 
In a summary, our present study revealed the protective role of conventional NK cells by 
regulating liver Mϕ and their polarization in the fibrosis progression of NASH, and that the 
mechanism responsible for the hepatic recruitment of NK cells involved the interaction of 
CXCL10 and CXCR3. These findings provide a better understanding of the immune pathogenesis 
of NASH.
